title: Better Things and the Limits of Wisdom

verses.text: A good name is better than fine perfume, and one's day of death is better than his day of birth.
It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart.
Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.
It is better to heed a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools.
For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This too is futile.
Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one.
Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool.
Do not say, "Why were the old days better than these?" For it is unwise of you to ask about this.
Wisdom, like an inheritance, is good, and it benefits those who see the sun.
For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner.
Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?
In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him.
In my futile life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness.
Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?
Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?
It is good to grasp the one and not let the other slip from your hand. For he who fears God will follow both warnings.
Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city.
Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
Do not pay attention to every word that is spoken, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom, saying, "I resolve to be wise." But it was beyond me.
What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?
I directed my mind to understand, to explore, to search out wisdom and explanations, and to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness.
And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared.
"Behold," says the Teacher, "I have discovered this by adding one thing to another to find an explanation.
While my soul was still searching but not finding, among a thousand I have found one upright man, but among all these I have not found one such woman.
Only this have I found: I have discovered that God made men upright, but they have sought out many schemes."

context.author: “The Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1); in Hebrew Qoheleth, “one who gathers” or “speaks to an assembly.” The book never names Solomon. Jewish and Christian tradition read it as Solomon; many scholars think a later writer took Solomon’s voice, because the Hebrew looks late and the speaker talks of kings before him in Jerusalem (1:16).
context.genre: Wisdom reflection: a searching first-person essay with poems and proverbs
context.audience: Anyone trying to find meaning in work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth, and finally “my son” (12:12)
context.setting: The second half of the book opens with a string of “better than” sayings: “A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth” (v.1). “It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting,” because death is the end of every man (v.2). A patient spirit is better than a proud one (v.8). “Do not say, ‘Why were the old days better than these?’” (v.10). In good days be joyful; in bad days remember that God made both (v.14). The Teacher has seen the righteous perish and the wicked live long (v.15), and he warns, “Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins” (v.20). He tried to be wise, “but it was beyond me” (v.23), and found only this: “God made men upright, but they have sought out many schemes” (v.29).
context.custom: Perfume and oil were precious, used at feasts and for burial; the Hebrew puts “name” (shem) and “perfume” (shemen) side by side in a play on words (v.1). Mourning lasted seven days, with friends visiting the house of the dead (Genesis 50:10; Job 2:13). Dry thorns burned fast and noisily under a cooking pot, then were gone (v.6).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 8 speaks of obeying the king and of justice delayed, and commends enjoying life.
context.timelineBible: Paul gathers verses like v.20 when he writes, “There is no one righteous, not even one” (Romans 3:10). Jesus says, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). Verse 29 looks back to Genesis 1-3.

translation.meaning: Name, reputation. A good name is better than fine perfume (shemen), a play on sounds.
Straight, right. God made people straight; they made themselves crooked.
Clever devices or inventions. Human ingenuity turned away from God.

gospelParallels.note: There is no one righteous, not even one.
Sin entered the world through one man.

otBackground.note: God saw all that He had made, and it was very good.
A good name is more desirable than great riches.

overview.summary: Sorrow and mourning teach more than feasting, patience beats pride, God made both good days and bad, no one is without sin, and wisdom itself is beyond reach.
overview.settingLine: A house of mourning and a house of feasting.

history.t: Seven days of grief in the house of the dead.

customs.t: Precious oil for feasts and burials.

archaeology.t: Small clay juglets for scented oil are common in Iron Age tombs.
An ancient perfume and balsam industry was based at Ein Gedi by the Dead Sea.

overview.discussion: “It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting” (v.2). What have times of grief taught me that good times never did?
overview.book: The book of Ecclesiastes · 12 chapters. The Teacher searches for lasting gain “under the sun,” finds everything a breath, and ends: fear God and keep His commandments.
overview.author: The Teacher (Qoheleth)

peoplePlaces.d: Their heart is in the house of mourning

historicalImage.caption: The Fall and Expulsion from the Garden of Eden, by Michelangelo (1509-10), Sistine Chapel. “God made men upright, but they have sought out many schemes” (Ecclesiastes 7:29); “all come from dust, and all return to dust” (3:20).

currentImage.caption: The rock-cut tomb of the priestly family of Hezir in the Kidron Valley, Jerusalem (2nd century BC). “Man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets” (Ecclesiastes 12:5).
